\chapter{Well}
\label{ch:la-well}
\hlchaptermodality{27}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can answer well in Latin with bene, and show how one regular sound change turns it into bien.}

Answer bene when asked how you fare, then derive bien from it in one regular sound change.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[bene]{bene — a morphologically simple inheritance}

\label{lesson:LA-C27-bene}



\begin{quote}
Last lesson's \textquotedblleft{}how\textquotedblright{} took a roundabout path into Romance, picking up an extra piece along the way. This one is refreshingly simple: one Latin word, one regular sound change, nothing grafted on.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: bene — \textquotedblleft{}well,\textquotedblright{} related to bonus}
\textbf{Bene} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{well}\textquotedblright{}) is a genuine Classical Latin adverb, closely related to \textbf{bonus} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{good}\textquotedblright{}) — both descend from the same \textbf{Old Latin} ancestor, \textbf{duenos/duonus} (found in the famous \textbf{Duenos inscription}, one of the oldest surviving Latin texts). Past that point, the ultimate Proto-Indo-European root is debated, with more than one proposal on the table.

\begin{cousinweb}
Here's the refreshing part: French's \textbf{bien} and Spanish's \textbf{bien} both continue \textbf{bene} through \textbf{one single, regular sound change} — short stressed \emph{e} diphthongizing to \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{ie},\textquotedblright{} the exact same shift behind \emph{mel} $\to$ \emph{miel} and \emph{terra} $\to$ \emph{tierra}/\emph{terre} — and \textbf{nothing else}. No extra suffix gets grafted on, unlike \emph{quōmodo}'s roundabout, multi-step journey into \emph{come}/\emph{cómo}/\emph{comment}. When two Romance languages agree this closely, picking up only one shared, ordinary sound change between them, you're looking almost straight at the Latin parent itself.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{Bene} is attested being used \textbf{alone}, repeated, in Plautus's \textbf{Stichus}, line 709 — though be honest about the context: it's a \textbf{drinking toast}, not literally an answer to \textquotedblleft{}how are you.\textquotedblright{} The characters raise their cups and say: \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}bene vōs, bene nōs, bene tē, bene mē, bene nostram etiam Stephanium\textquotedblright{}} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{well to you, well to us, well to you, well to me, well to our Stephanium too}.\textquotedblright{} A real, attested use of \emph{bene} standing alone — just repurposed here for the same conversational slot \textquotedblleft{}well\textquotedblright{} fills, the way \emph{volup est convēnisse} was for \textquotedblleft{}nice to meet you.\textquotedblright{}
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}

  \item \textquotedblleft{}bene\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}well,\textquotedblright{} related to bonus
  \item the morphologically simple inheritance — French/Spanish bien is bene plus one regular sound change, nothing grafted on
  \item the honest context — bene vōs, bene nōs... is a drinking toast in Plautus, not literally \textquotedblleft{}how are you\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

What Latin word is French and Spanish's \textbf{bien}, continued through one regular sound change?
